title: Younger workers’ job-finding expectations fell behind realized hiring rates after the pandemic
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: New York Fed researchers compare two answers to the same practical question. If an employed worker lost a job, how likely would that person be to find another within three months? The Survey of Consumer Expectations asks employed respondents for that probability. The authors use the Current Population Survey to observe what happened to people who had actually been unemployed and looking for work for four weeks or less. The measures were close before the pandemic. Since 2022, workers’ stated prospects have trailed observed re-employment rates. The comparison uses separate samples, so it establishes a gap between group averages and cannot establish whether any particular respondent misjudged their own prospects (job-finding section and first chart).

Over 2014–2019, expected three-month job finding averaged 55.5%, against an observed rate of 57.2%. The first chart plots six-month moving averages. Because the observed rate looks forward from the start of unemployment, the pandemic lowered realized re-employment prospects for some workers who became unemployed before its onset. Respondents’ expectations fell when the pandemic arrived in March 2020. After 2020 the observed series largely recovered to pre-pandemic levels by 2021. Since 2022 it has averaged 58.8% while respondents’ expectations have averaged 53.0%. The gap persisted after the abrupt interruption that briefly sent the two measures in different directions.

The change was concentrated among younger and less-educated workers. The second chart compares January 2014–June 2019 with January 2022–March 2026. Respondents aged 30 or younger went from expecting job-finding rates 6.3 percentage points above observed rates to expecting rates 3.0 points below them. For those with a high-school education or less, expectations had been close to observed rates before the pandemic, then fell 7.5 points below them. Workers over 30 already underestimated job-finding prospects by 5.4 points before the pandemic and by 6.1 points afterward. For those with at least some college, the corresponding shortfalls were 4.6 and 4.0 points. The age and education categories overlap. Their contributions cannot simply be added.

Job loss is harder to compare. The expectations survey asks separately about layoffs and voluntary departures over twelve months. The authors convert expected job loss to a three-month horizon. In the employment data they count an exit as a loss when employment ends within three months and the first state afterward is unemployment, meaning the person is without work and searching. This rule misses a layoff followed by an exit from the labour force and may miss someone who anticipates a layoff and quits first. The authors accordingly describe their measure as a lower bound. The observed probability is roughly half the expected one, but that difference alone cannot establish excessive pessimism (job-loss section and third chart).

Tenure provides another clue. The fourth chart compares perceived and observed risk by time on the job. The observed probability of loss falls more steeply with tenure than workers’ reported risk. After two years with the employer, expected loss is more than twice its observed counterpart. The tenure comparison omits mid-2019 through the end of 2021, when separation rates were unusually high. Together the results show why a household survey can signal insecurity even when hiring or retention looks more favourable in an aggregate series. Whether that divergence changes household spending or job search is a further empirical question. The article and its accompanying data do not estimate those behavioural effects.

questions.question: Would following the same workers narrow the gap between expected and realized re-employment?
questions.detail: The survey asks employed workers about a hypothetical loss, whereas the realized outcome concerns people already unemployed and searching. Their exposure to occupations, industries, and local hiring conditions may differ. Match these characteristics across samples or follow individual survey respondents after actual displacement. That comparison would help distinguish changes in subjective beliefs from changes in the mix of workers who experience unemployment.

questions.question: Why did expectations change especially sharply among younger and less-educated workers?
questions.detail: The age and education comparisons are shown separately, and the same worker can fall into both groups. Examine their joint distribution, along with occupation, local unemployment and previous layoff experience. Test whether the change survives comparable sample weights across the two periods. Distinguishing changes in the opportunity set from changes in beliefs matters when using sentiment surveys to assess households’ willingness to spend.

questions.question: How much of the tenure gap survives a broader definition of involuntary job loss?
questions.detail: The authors’ realized measure excludes some moves into inactivity and quits before expected layoffs. Reconstruct separations using information about termination reasons, direct employer-to-employer moves and labour-force exits. Then compare the expected and realized profiles for each tenure group on a common horizon. A large remaining gap would support the interpretation that workers underestimate how much their job security improves with tenure.
